read.sections.0.heading.source: A model learns from labelled examples
read.sections.0.heading.back: A model learns from labelled examples

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI learns a bit like studying with flashcards. At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data: pictures of leaves, each with the correct answer, called a label, either “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses these examples to build a model. It uses the model to predict the label of a leaf it has never seen. This is machine learning. Nobody writes the rule “spots mean sick”; the computer finds patterns like that in the examples. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning, one kind of machine learning. It is an old idea. A machine called the perceptron learned from marked cards in 1958, and researchers studied this lesson's method in 1967. It became far more useful after 2010, with more data and faster computers.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI learns a bit like revising a lesson with flashcards. At the Sunrise garden people collected training data, which is photos of leaves, each photo with a correct answer called a label: “healthy” or “diseased”. The computer uses these examples to build a model, then uses that model to predict the label of a leaf it has never seen before. This is machine learning. No one wrote the rule “spots mean diseased”; the computer found patterns like that itself from the examples. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning, which is one kind of machine learning. This is an old idea: a machine called the perceptron learned from marked cards back in 1958, and researchers studied the method used in this lesson in 1967. The method became hugely more useful after 2010, when there was more data and computers were faster.
read.sections.0.text.note: flashcards: บัตรคำ, the classroom word. Also in watch.summary.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data. Each leaf picture has the right answer, called a label: “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses them to make a model. It uses the model to guess. This is machine learning. Nobody tells it “spots mean sick”. It finds that in the examples. Learning from labels is called supervised learning. It is an old idea. A machine did it in 1958. This method was studied in 1967. It grew more useful after 2010.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: At the Sunrise garden people collected training data. Each leaf photo has a correct answer, called a label: “healthy” or “diseased”. The computer uses these photos to build a model. It uses the model to guess. This is machine learning. No one told it “spots mean diseased”. It found this itself from the examples. Learning from labels is called supervised learning. This is an old idea. In 1958 there was already a machine that could do this. In 1967 people studied this method. After 2010 it became more useful.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Better examples, then a fair test
read.sections.1.heading.back: Better examples, then a fair test

read.sections.1.text.source: The first model learned from only two examples. It guesses in a simple way: it finds the example most like the new leaf and copies its label. On six new leaves it got four right. It called a small, light green leaf “sick”, because it had too few examples to compare with. Then the team added four leaves that looked different, and it got all six right. But the team had already looked at those six test leaves while they improved the model. A fair test uses leaves that nobody has used yet. The team kept four leaves aside. The model got three of them right. It called a long leaf that was turning yellow “healthy”. A fresh test shows what a model still gets wrong. Four leaves are still a small test.
read.sections.1.text.back: The first model learned from only two examples. It guessed in a simple way: find the example most like the new leaf and copy that example's label. Tested on six new leaves, it got four right. It said the small light green young leaf was “diseased”, because there were too few examples to compare with. Then the team added four more leaves that looked different, and it got all six right. But the team had already looked at those six test leaves while improving the model. A fair test needs leaves no one has used yet. So the team kept four leaves aside, and the model got three right. It said the long yellowing leaf was “healthy”. Testing with new leaves showed where the model still makes mistakes, and four leaves is still a small test.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: The first model had only two examples. It finds the example most like a new leaf. It copies that label. It got four of six new leaves right. It had too few examples. Then the team added four different leaves. Now it got all six right. But the team had already seen those six leaves. A fair test uses new leaves. The team kept four leaves aside. The model got three of them right. A new test shows what it still gets wrong.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: The first model had only two leaf examples. It found the example most like the new leaf, then copied that label. It got four of six new leaves right, because it had too few examples. Then the team added four more different leaves. Now it got all six right. But the team had already seen those six leaves. A fair test needs new leaves. The team kept four leaves aside. The model got three right. The new test tells where it still makes mistakes.

read.sections.2.heading.back: An example from the real world

read.sections.2.text.source: Real tools work in a similar way, at a much bigger size. In Tanzania, researchers from the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Penn State University made a free phone app called Nuru. It learned from pictures of the leaves of cassava, a food crop, taken in Tanzanian fields, and it works without the internet. When researchers tested it on plants in the field, it did much better when it looked at six leaves from a plant than at one. Relevant examples with correct labels help a model. More examples alone do not always help: a wrong label can make guesses worse. And a tool like this only helps people check leaves. Farmers and experts still decide what to do.
read.sections.2.text.back: Real tools work in a similar way, but are much bigger. In Tanzania, researchers from the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Penn State University built a free phone app called Nuru. The app learned from photos of cassava leaves, a food plant, taken in Tanzanian fields, and it works even without internet. When researchers tested it on cassava plants in fields, the app did much better when it looked at six leaves from the same plant instead of just one. Examples that match the task and have correct labels help a model, but more examples alone do not always help, because wrong labels can make guesses worse. And a tool like this only helps people check leaves; farmers and experts still decide what to do next.
read.sections.2.text.note: International Institute of Tropical Agriculture: written as สถาบันเกษตรเขตร้อนนานาชาติ (no English, as the reading is read aloud); Penn State kept in Latin. Tanzania: แทนซาเนีย, cassava: มันสำปะหลัง.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Real tools work like this too, but they are much bigger. In Tanzania, researchers made a free phone app called Nuru. It learned from pictures of cassava leaves. Cassava is a plant that people grow for food. It works without the internet. In tests, it did better when it looked at six leaves from a plant. Good examples with the right labels help. A wrong label can make it worse. The app helps people check leaves. People still decide what to do.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Real tools work like this too, but much bigger. In Tanzania researchers built a free phone app called Nuru. It learned from photos of cassava leaves. watch.summary.source: This video explains computer vision. Computer vision is how a computer finds meaning in pictures. A computer does not see a picture like you do. It sees a number for each tiny dot of colour. Writing exact rules for a shape, like the letter X, does not work well, because people draw an X in many ways. With machine learning, the computer learns from many labelled examples instead. It is like learning with flashcards. The computer guesses, checks the answer and slowly gets better. Harder pictures, like faces, need bigger models. The video shows farm robots that tell crops from weeds. It also warns about a problem. If the training data leaves some people out, the tool can fail for them. So training data must be large and varied.
watch.summary.back: This video explains computer vision, which is how computers find meaning in pictures. A computer does not see a picture the way you do: it sees one number for each tiny dot of colour. Writing exact rules for a shape, such as the letter X, does not work well, because people draw X in many ways. In machine learning the computer learns from many labelled examples instead, like studying with flashcards. The computer guesses, checks the answer and slowly gets better. Harder pictures, such as faces, need bigger models. The video shows a farm robot that tells crops from weeds, and also warns of a problem: if the training data does not include some groups of people, the tool may not work for those groups. So training data must be large and varied.

educatorNotes.1.source: The model is deliberately simple: a nearest-neighbour model (k = 1) that copies the label of the most similar example. It is one supervised method; Cover and Hart's 1967 paper studied this rule, and Rosenblatt's perceptron, shown in July 1958, also learned from labelled examples. Real AI is far bigger, and other kinds of machine learning don't need a label on every example, but the points about examples and testing are the same.
educatorNotes.1.back: This model is deliberately simple: a nearest-neighbour model (k = 1) that copies the label of the most similar example. This is one supervised method. Cover and Hart's 1967 paper studied this rule, and Rosenblatt's perceptron, shown in July 1958, also learned from labelled examples. Real AI is much bigger, and other kinds of machine learning do not need a label on every example, but the points about examples and testing stay the same.

educatorNotes.2.source: Nuru: the evaluation in Tanzania (Mrisho and others, a bioRxiv preprint from 2020) found the app more accurate with six leaves per plant than with one leaf image. The lesson gives no percentages on purpose: the study's numbers depend on which test and which disease. The app supports diagnosis; it does not replace extension workers or farmers' decisions.
educatorNotes.2.back: Nuru: an evaluation in Tanzania (Mrisho et al., bioRxiv preprint, 2020) found the app was more accurate using six leaves per plant compared with a single leaf photo. The lesson deliberately gives no percentages, because the figures in the study depend on the kind of test and the disease. The app helps diagnosis but does not replace agricultural extension workers or farmers' decisions.

educatorNotes.3.source: If a learner labels an example differently from the gardener in the extension, the model follows the learner. That is a good moment to ask: who decides the right label?
educatorNotes.3.back: If learners label examples differently from the gardener in the extra activity, the model follows the learner. That is a good moment to ask: who decides which label is right?
